title: Skinning and Dressing of Small Stock Carcasses using the Traditional or Inverted Skinning and Dressing of Small Stock Carcasses using either the Traditional or Inverted Slaughtering Method

lessons.title: Skinning hygiene and first steps
lessons.html:
The aim of skinning

Skinning removes the skin (pelt) from the carcass without letting wool, hair or dirt touch the meat, and without cutting the skin, fat or meat. A good skin also has value: it is sold to tanneries. Holes in the skin lower its price.

The golden rules

  • The outside of the skin must never touch the meat.
  • Keep one hand for the outside of the skin and one hand for the meat side, as your trainer shows you.
  • Sterilise your knife after each cut through the skin, because cutting from the outside drags germs in.
  • Cut from the inside of the skin outwards wherever possible.
  • Wash hands often.

First steps (both methods)

  1. Remove the front feet at the knee joint and the hind feet at the hock joint, as your plant does it. Some plants remove feet after the legs have been skinned.
  2. Head: skin the head or remove it at the atlas joint as your plant procedure says. Keep the head matched to the carcass for inspection.
  3. Open the skin along the legs and down the middle of the neck and chest, with the knife pointing outwards.
  4. Tie the oesophagus (weasand) so stomach contents cannot leak from the throat.
  5. Free the skin from the legs, brisket and shoulders by hand (fisting) or with the knife, keeping the skin folded away from the meat.

Use your fist to push the skin off where you can. Fisting causes fewer cuts in the meat and the skin than a knife.

lessons.title: The traditional and inverted methods
lessons.html:
Traditional method

In the traditional method the carcass hangs by the hind legs for dressing. The skin is freed around the hind legs, the tail and the back end first, and then pulled downwards towards the head, over the shoulders and neck.

  • The rectum and the back end are worked on early.
  • The skin is pulled down over the carcass, so take care that the woolly side falls away from the meat.

Inverted method

In the inverted method the carcass is moved so that it hangs by the front legs. The skin is freed at the front first (brisket, shoulders, neck) and then pulled downwards over the back and hindquarters, off the hind legs and tail.

  • The skin rolls downward away from the meat, which helps to keep wool off the carcass.
  • Many modern small stock lines use the inverted method because it is more hygienic and can be done at line speed with a mechanical skin puller.

Comparing the methods

TraditionalInverted
Carcass hangs byHind legsFront legs
Skin removedFrom back end towards headFrom front towards back end
Main riskWool touching meat as skin is pulled over the shouldersWool touching the hindquarters if the pull is not controlled

Both methods are acceptable when done well. Follow the method and steps your abattoir uses.

lessons.title: Finishing the dressing
lessons.html:
After skinning

  1. Check for wool and dirt. Any wool, hair or dirt on the carcass must be trimmed off with a sterile knife. Do not just wash it.
  2. Free and tie the rectum (bung) so dung cannot come out, if not already done.
  3. Open the belly carefully with the knife blade pointing outwards and the guts protected by your hand.
  4. Eviscerate: remove the rough offal (stomachs and intestines) and then the red offal (pluck: heart, lungs, liver, and often the windpipe and throat). Keep them matched to the carcass.
  5. Present for inspection: carcass, head and organs together for the meat inspector.
  6. Trim and wash after inspection, as the procedure says.

Skin handling

  • Put skins in the skin chute or bin straight away. Do not drop them on the walkway.
  • Keep skins away from carcasses.
  • Skins are salted or sent off as your plant arranges.

Common faults and how to avoid them

FaultPrevention
Wool on meatKeep the skin folded away; use the two-hand rule
Knife cuts in meat or skin (scores)Use fisting; keep the knife flat; work steadily
Torn fat coverPull the skin steadily, not in jerks
Gut cut during openingBlade outwards; protect the guts with your hand

Key points

  • The outside of the skin must never touch the meat.
  • Traditional method: hung by the hind legs, skin removed towards the head.
  • Inverted method: hung by the front legs, skin removed towards the back end.
  • Use fisting to free the skin and cut from the inside outwards.
  • Trim off wool and dirt; do not just wash it.
  • Keep the head, organs and carcass matched for inspection.
